speaker: Unknown
en: Trailer
zh: 预告片

speaker: Eric Simons
en: People are not losing their jobs because of AI, at least certainly not to the degree some AI leaders said it was going to happen. What's actually going on, though, is...
zh: 人们并没有因为 AI 而失去工作，至少肯定没有达到某些 AI 领袖所说的那种程度。不过，实际正在发生的是……

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
en: I was driving around and I saw a billboard by your company that said...
zh: 我开车在路上，看到你们公司的一块广告牌，上面写着……

speaker: Eric Simons
en: The team was like 10 or 12 people at that time, and overnight we just woke up with tens of thousands, or hundreds of thousands, of paying customers.
zh: 当时团队大概只有 10 到 12 个人，然后一夜之间，我们一觉醒来就有了数万甚至数十万的付费客户。

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
en: Eric Simons, CEO of Bolt. I saw a post you made a few weeks ago that said your best advice is "don't die." I think that is so powerful.
zh: Eric Simons,Bolt 的 CEO。几周前我看到你发的一个帖子，说你最好的建议是「别死」。我觉得这句话非常有力量。

speaker: Eric Simons
en: We launched in October of 2024, and in the first month we went from zero to five million of ARR.
zh: 我们在 2024 年 10 月上线，第一个月我们从零做到了 500 万美元的 ARR。

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
en: And back in the day, the whole winning strategy was you have to be hyper, hyper specific: analytics, product roadmap. And now it's about a platform.
zh: 而在以前，整个制胜策略是必须超级、超级细分：分析、产品路线图。而现在是关于一个平台。

speaker: Eric Simons
en: There are only two ways to make money in the software business. Introduction
zh: 在软件行业，赚钱的方式只有两种。引言

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
en: Hey, this is Carlos, CEO at Product School and your host on The Product Podcast. My guest today is Eric Simons, CEO of StackBlitz, the company behind Bolt, and I'm a user of the product. He skipped college, spent seven years getting to half a million dollars in ARR, and had a board meeting scheduled to wind the company down. One month before that meeting, they launched Bolt and went from half a million to $5.5 million in 30 days, with a team of 12. Here's what we'll cover: the pivot that happened one month before the shutdown meeting. Why the cloud IDE market turned out to be a mirage. His Yahoo and AOL warning for everyone building everything. Why he signed the open weights letter. And the billboard apologizing for the SaaS apocalypse. Let's get into it.
zh: 嘿，我是 Carlos,Product School 的 CEO,也是 The Product Podcast 的主持人。今天的嘉宾是 Eric Simons,StackBlitz——也就是 Bolt 背后的那家公司——的 CEO,而我是这款产品的用户。他跳过了大学，花了七年才做到 50 万美元 ARR,当时已经安排好了一场解散公司的董事会会议。在那场会议的一个月前，他们上线了 Bolt,并在 30 天内从 50 万美元涨到了 550 万美元 ARR,团队只有 12 个人。以下是我们将聊到的内容：解散会议前一个月的转型。为什么云 IDE 市场最终成了一场幻影。他给每一个「什么都做」的人的 Yahoo 和 AOL 警告。他为什么签署开放权重公开信。还有那块为 SaaS 末日道歉的广告牌。我们开始吧。

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
en: Welcome to The Product Podcast, Eric.
zh: 欢迎来到 The Product Podcast,Eric。

speaker: Eric Simons
en: Thank you for having me. I'm excited to be here.
zh: 谢谢你们邀请我。我很高兴能来到这里。

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
en: I'm excited to have you, because I'm a user of your product, and it's always great to put a face to the name and learn more about the story behind the scenes.
zh: 我也很高兴邀请到你，因为我是你们产品的用户，能见到名字背后的面孔、了解更多幕后故事总是很棒。

speaker: Eric Simons
en: Yeah, awesome. I'm excited to dig in. Startups Are an Endurance Sport
zh: 是啊，太好了。我很期待深入聊聊。创业是一项耐力运动

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
en: Last time we spoke, you were wearing an Ironman hat. I know you're big into sports, so maybe we can start there.
zh: 上次我们聊的时候，你戴着一顶 Ironman 的帽子。我知道你对体育很热衷，也许我们可以从这里开始。

speaker: Eric Simons
en: Yeah, I have my Ironman hat over here, I can put it on if you want. So, what do you want to know about the sports side?
zh: 是啊，我有一顶 Ironman 的帽子就在这儿，你要是想的话我可以戴上。那么，关于体育这一块你想知道什么？

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
en: I'm obsessed with sports too, but I think you take it one step up. There's a story that connects with your upbringing. I know you're a high school dropout, and you've always been looking for a hard path in a way. So tell us more about what drives you so much to not give up.
zh: 我也对体育很着迷，但我觉得你比我更进一步。有一个和你成长经历相关的故事。我知道你是高中辍学的，从某种意义上说，你一直都在寻找一条艰难的路。所以跟我们讲讲，是什么让你如此坚定地不放弃。

speaker: Eric Simons
en: Yeah. Well, my parents would have shot me if I'd dropped out of high school, so I finished high school, but then instead of going to college, I started doing startups. I think I tend to look at how I want to approach life in a very first-principles sort of way. That's an overused term at this point, but for where I grew up, the city of Chicago, back in the late 2000s the thing was: you graduate high school, you go to college, you get a job. That was the path. There were no other kids I grew up with who did not do the college thing. My co-founder and I actually grew up down the street from each other. I think we were 13 when we learned how to code together. By the time we came to graduate, I was like, we're going to have to pay for college out of pocket, and it was going to cost, for University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, something like $30,000 a year in-state. And we thought, this doesn't make a lot of sense. We were making, I think, maybe 50 bucks an hour at that time, at 17 or 18, writing software. So to me it just seemed obvious: what am I going to go to college to learn? I'm writing software. I can learn, but I can read textbooks, and that's free. It's kind of the Good Will Hunting thing, not that I'm anywhere close to the IQ of that character Matt Damon played. But to me it was just going and doing what seemed obvious, and that's not priced in. The whole college-as-default-path thing, many people are questioning it, which I think is a good thing. Especially if you're going to do business, if you're starting startups, you're not going to have a good time with it. You'll quit pretty early on if you don't develop a lot of grit and resilience, because that's kind of the entire game. This is an endurance sport, and it's about pushing through pain. A couple of years ago I got into doing Ironmans, and it's very analogous: you have to be going for very long stretches, and it's not even about race day, it's about all of the training that goes into it. You're spending six hours a day, every weekend, for six months leading up to that thing. And startups are the same: it's not about one big launch, it's about every day putting in the work, embracing pain, and pushing through it. That's how I view these things.
zh: 是的。嗯，如果我高中辍学，我父母会毙了我的，所以我读完了高中，但之后我没有去上大学，而是开始做创业公司。我觉得我倾向于用一种非常第一性原理的方式来看待我该如何对待人生。这个词现在已经用滥了，但对于我成长的地方，芝加哥，在 2000 年代后期，事情是这样的：你高中毕业，你上大学，你找一份工作。那就是既定的路。我从小到大认识的孩子里没有一个不走上大学这条路的。我和我的联合创始人其实就是在同一条街上长大的。我们大概 13 岁的时候一起学会了编程。到我们要毕业的时候，我心想，我们得自掏腰包付大学学费，而对于伊利诺伊大学香槟分校，本州学费一年大概要三万美元。我们觉得，这不太划算。我们当时 17、18 岁，写软件大概能挣每小时 50 美元。所以对我来说答案很明显：我去大学能学到什么？我就在写软件。我可以学，但我可以读教科书，而那是免费的。这有点像《心灵捕手》里的情节，不是说我的智商能和 Matt Damon 演的那个角色相比。但对我来说，这就是去做那件显而易见、却没被市场定价的事情。「上大学是默认路径」这整套观念，现在很多人都在质疑，我觉得这是件好事。尤其如果你要做生意、要做创业公司，你不会过得轻松。如果你不培养出大量的韧性和抗挫折能力，你很早就退出了，因为这基本上就是整个游戏。这是一项耐力运动，关键在于挺过痛苦。几年前我开始参加 Ironman 铁人三项，道理非常类似：你必须坚持很长很长的时间，而且关键甚至不在比赛当天，而在于为此付出的所有训练。在那之前的六个月里，你每天花六个小时，每个周末都在练。创业公司也是一样：关键不在于某一次大发布，而在于每一天都在投入工作，拥抱痛苦，并挺过去。这就是我看待这些事情的方式。

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
en: I love that connection you made between sports and business. I feel the same way. I saw a post you made a few weeks ago that said the best advice is "don't die," and I think that is so powerful, because sometimes the pressure is on growing fast at all costs, or winning the short term, but in reality, staying in the game, finding ways to not die, compounds much more than trying to win the sprint.
zh: 我很喜欢你把体育和商业联系起来的这个类比。我也有同感。几周前我看到你发的一个帖子，说你最好的建议是「别死」，我觉得这句话非常有力量，因为有时候压力都在于不惜一切代价快速增长，或者赢得短期竞争，但实际上，留在牌桌上、想办法不死，远比试图赢下短跑冲刺更有复利效应。

speaker: Eric Simons
en: Yeah, totally. Over the past year and a half, there have been a lot of short-term strategies in the space. Every time this happens in business, there are these moments where you have manias, where you can do very short-sighted things and maybe walk away financially up. The problem, from my view, is: you're going to build a business, so why do this if you're not trying to build something that's actually durable for the long term? You've got to do it the right way, because otherwise it's a pretty high-risk endeavor for you, and certainly for anyone else working for you. So it's the quote of "play long-term games with long-term people." I think that's a good quote, and I believe in it. The Pivot One Month Before Shutdown
zh: 是的，完全同意。在过去一年半里，这个领域出现了很多短期策略。商业世界里每当这种情况发生，总会有狂热的时刻，你可以做非常短视的事情，也许还能在财务上赚一笔离场。在我看来，问题在于：你要做的是一门生意，如果你不是想打造一个真正长期耐用的东西，那为什么要做？你必须用正确的方式去做，否则这对你是高风险的赌注，对任何为你工作的人更是如此。所以就是那句名言：「和长期主义者玩长期游戏。」我觉得这句话很好，我也相信它。解散会议前一个月的转型

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
en: Let's talk about your product and your business. Even your current company is called Bolt, but that wasn't the original name, right? StackBlitz was the original name, and you actually started the company before AI was mainstream. So tell me more about that major pivot you had to do to take the AI tailwinds and make sure you're in the position you are today, at a scale of around $700 million in valuation.
zh: 我们聊聊你的产品和你的生意吧。你现在公司叫 Bolt,但这不是最初的名字，对吧？最初的名字是 StackBlitz,而且你创办这家公司的时候 AI 还没成为主流。所以跟我说说那次重大转型，你是如何借助 AI 的东风，走到今天这个位置的——估值大约 7 亿美元。

speaker: Eric Simons
en: Yeah. So we've been around a while. We started StackBlitz, which is the underlying company behind Bolt, in 2017. The insight we had was that browsers had become very powerful, and it seemed technologically possible to bring full-stack web development to the web. In the same way that Figma brought design to the web for the first time, the idea that you could come into just a browser, without downloading anything, and actually be building real full-stack applications from a browser tab, was possible for the first time. We wrote some really cool technology. We basically wrote an operating system that runs in WebAssembly in your browser. Very nerdy stuff, but no one had ever done it before, and it took us three or four years to build. We launched it in 2021, into the cloud IDE market. At that time, in the late 2010s and early 2020s, there was all this hype around cloud IDEs, but it ended up being a mirage of a market: a lot of hype, but people weren't willing to spend money, because developers were very happy with their local environments. Fast forward to 2024, and us and all the other cloud IDE companies were on the rocks. We had to figure out what we were going to do. We'd set the target that we had to inflect revenue, we had to prove this was a venture-scale business, otherwise we'd start winding the company down by the end of the year. So through 2024 we tried out a whole bunch of different ideas, different product shapes we thought would be interesting and that customers would like. And none of them worked. Bolt was actually the last product idea we tried. We launched in October of 2024, and our board meeting was one month later, where we were going to start spinning down the company. In the first month, we went from zero to five million of ARR. Before that, we'd spent seven years getting to 500K, half a million, of ARR, and then in 30 days we went from 0.5 to 5.5 million of ARR. And then the month after, we went from 5.5 to 20.5 million or something. So it was just crazy. Our team was like 10 or 12 people at that time, and overnight we woke up with tens of thousands, or hundreds of thousands, of paying customers. Growing into that scale was insane. But that's kind of the story of how Bolt came to be.
zh: 是的。我们存在挺久了。我们在 2017 年创办了 StackBlitz,也就是 Bolt 背后的公司。我们的洞察是，浏览器已经变得非常强大，从技术上讲，把全栈 Web 开发搬到 web 上似乎是可以做到的。就像 Figma 第一次把设计搬上了 web,你不下载任何东西，直接打开一个浏览器标签页，就能真正构建全栈应用——这在历史上是第一次成为可能。我们写了一些非常酷的技术。我们基本上写了一个能在浏览器里的 WebAssembly 上运行的操作系统。非常极客的东西，但以前从没人做过，我们花了三四年才建好。我们在 2021 年发布，进入了云 IDE 市场。那个时候，2010 年代末到 2020 年代初，围绕云 IDE 有各种炒作，但这个市场最终成了一场幻影：炒作很多，但人们不愿意花钱，因为开发者对自己的本地环境非常满意。快进到 2024 年，我们和其他所有云 IDE 公司都陷入了困境。我们必须想办法。我们设定了目标：必须让营收出现拐点，必须证明这是一门风投规模的生意，否则到年底我们就开始解散公司。所以在 2024 年全年，我们尝试了一大堆不同的点子，各种我们认为有意思、客户会喜欢的产品形态。但没有一个成功。Bolt 其实是我们尝试的最后一个产品点子。我们在 2024 年 10 月上线，而一个月后就是董事会会议，我们本来打算在那个会上开始解散公司。第一个月，我们从零做到了 500 万美元 ARR。在此之前，我们花了七年才做到 50 万美元——也就是五十万美元的 ARR,然后在 30 天内，我们从 50 万涨到了 550 万美元 ARR。而再下一个月，我们从 550 万涨到了 2050 万美元左右。简直是疯了。当时我们团队大概 10 到 12 个人，一夜之间醒来就有了数万甚至数十万的付费客户。在那种规模下成长起来简直不可思议。但这基本上就是 Bolt 诞生的故事。

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
en: Speaking of product-market fit, it's hard to pick an official definition, but like you just said, when the market is pulling, that is ultimately the best validation.
zh: 说到产品市场契合，很难给出一个官方定义，但就像你刚才说的，当市场在拉着你走，那归根结底就是最好的验证。

speaker: Eric Simons
en: Absolutely. I've worked on a lot of things in my career, and I've never seen anything like what happened there. There are a number of companies now that have had these zero-to-explosive revenue ramps, but we were the first thing that hit the market that anyone had seen do this. In the AI era there have now been more of these, but being the first one was an interesting experience, because normally the playbook to grow the team of a company that's at 20 million of ARR gives you a minimum of two years to prepare. That happened in two months for us. There were no playbooks, so we ended up having to create new playbooks on how to deal with this kind of scale this quickly. It was a fun and very challenging experience. Focusing on B2B and Product Builders
zh: 完全正确。我职业生涯里做过很多事情，我从没见过那里发生的那种情况。现在有不少公司都经历了这种从零到爆发的营收增长，但我们是第一个做到这件事并让市场看到的公司。在 AI 时代现在已经有了更多这样的案例，但做第一个是一种很特别的体验，因为通常来说，给一家 ARR 达到 2000 万美元的公司扩充团队的常规操作，会给你至少两年的准备时间。而我们这一切发生在两个月之内。没有任何现成的打法，所以我们最终不得不为如何应对这种快速到来的规模创造新的打法。这是一段有趣也极具挑战的经历。聚焦 B2B 和产品构建者

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
en: Moving forward, you raised over $100 million at a valuation of around 700 million. So what is the current state of your business?
zh: 往前说，你们以约 7 亿美元的估值融资超过 1 亿美元。那你们目前业务的现状是怎样的？

speaker: Eric Simons
en: Yeah. When we first launched, we had lots of different types of customers using the product. What we've gotten very focused on is how we really help very specific types of users and workflows. PMs and product folks are one of the key ones. So we're really focusing on the B2B side of the business and doing a great job on the product-development workflows folks use on Bolt. That's been a key focal point. Our B2B revenue year over year is up significantly; it's the fastest-growing segment of revenue for the company, and that's where we've been focusing all of our time.
zh: 是的。我们刚上线的时候，有各种不同类型的客户在使用产品。而我们如今非常聚焦的是，如何真正帮助非常特定类型的用户和工作流。PM 和产品人员是其中最关键的群体之一。所以我们真正聚焦在业务的 B2B 一侧，把人们在 Bolt 上使用的产品开发工作流做到极致。这一直是关键焦点。我们的 B2B 营收同比大幅增长；它是公司增长最快的营收板块，也是我们把全部时间投入的地方。

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
en: As I think about the category you in a way pioneered, this cloud IDE that then turned into AI prototyping tools, and then evolved into full-on end-to-end coding tools, what is the current state, and where do you think it's going?
zh: 当我想到你在某种程度上开创的这个品类——这个后来变成 AI 原型工具、再演化成完整的端到端编程工具的云 IDE——目前的现状是怎样的？你觉得它会走向哪里？

speaker: Eric Simons
en: Yeah, for vibe coding in general, you mean?
zh: 好的，你是指 vibe coding 整体而言吧？

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
en: Yeah. I see a lot of these companies in your category just letting users prototype something that looks cute, that was more of a demo. But then you evolved into a real solution that allows deployment into production. So it's not a toy anymore; this actually works. So first I want to learn more about what's going on, and then where you think this is going next.
zh: 对。我看到你这个品类的很多公司只是让用户做出一些看起来可爱、更像演示的东西。但你们演化成了一个能部署到生产环境的真正的解决方案。所以它不再是玩具了；这是真能用的东西。所以我想先多了解一下现在的情况，然后听听你觉得接下来会走向哪里。

speaker: Eric Simons
en: For sure. I think a lot of the core use cases you're describing are going to continue, and there's going to be a lot more depth to the workflows. For example, as a PM or a designer, I want to be able to rapidly iterate on how the experience should feel. It's actually useful to do that in an environment detached from your production environment, because it's way faster to iterate and get that feedback. But the problem is, if you do it outside of your production codebase, how do you marry that back into the production codebase in a way that your engineering team signs off on? So the stuff we've been working on is creating a very seamless connection: using the exact production components, and having a seamless handoff flow to developers where it automatically pulls in your changes. I think we're going to see more depth of integrations and workflows that pave out those experiences. On the flip side, we have a lot of entrepreneurs who use our product to build their businesses. We have lots of entrepreneurs generating millions of dollars on our product. So how do you further enable people to do that? What are the types of applications they're trying to make, or would want to make, and how do you make our agent the best in the world at doing those things? Those are kind of intertwined, because what is a prototype but a proposal to ship functionality into your real production codebase? And perhaps that production codebase is in Bolt, or perhaps it's not. But that's how we're seeing these things evolve. Positioning in the Vibe-Coding Landscape
zh: 没问题。我觉得你描述的很多核心用例会继续存在，而且这些工作流会有更多的深度。举例来说，作为 PM 或设计师，我想快速迭代「这个体验应该是什么感觉」。在一个和生产环境分离的环境里做这件事其实是很有用的，因为迭代和拿到反馈的速度快得多。但问题是，如果你在生产代码库之外做这件事，你怎么把它重新嫁接回生产代码库，并且让工程团队签字认可？所以我们一直在做的，就是打造一个非常无缝的连接：使用完全一样的生产组件，并提供一个无缝的交接流程给开发者，自动把你的改动拉进去。我认为我们会看到更深的集成和工作流来铺平这些体验。另一方面，我们有很多创业者用我们的产品来经营他们的生意。我们有很多创业者靠我们的产品赚到了数百万美元。那么如何进一步赋能他们？他们想做、或想做的应用类型是什么，以及怎么让我们的智能体成为世界上做这些事最厉害的？这些其实是交织在一起的，因为一个原型是什么？不就是一份把功能发布到你真实生产代码库的提案吗？而这个生产代码库可能在 Bolt 里，也可能不在。但这就是我们看到这些事情演化的方式。在 Vibe Coding 格局中的定位

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
en: I see the competitive landscape evolving that way. The analogy here is in LLMs: ChatGPT got the first-mover advantage and grew within consumer, while Anthropic grew within enterprise. Now of course they're converging, but they kind of picked lanes at the beginning. In your world, the vibe-coding world, you see other companies like Replit and Lovable, and there are always new ones popping up like mushrooms. So how do you position your product?
zh: 我看到竞争格局正是这样演化的。这里的类比可以看 LLM:ChatGPT 拿到了先发优势，在消费端增长，而 Anthropic 在企业端增长。现在它们当然在趋同，但它们一开始各自选了赛道。在你的世界——vibe coding 的世界——你看到 Replit、Lovable 这样的其他公司，而且总有新公司像蘑菇一样冒出来。那你们如何定位自己的产品？

speaker: Eric Simons
en: It's a really good question. Over the past year, I think it was about a year ago, we made the decision to orient more toward people building products professionally at businesses. There are a lot of people excited about AI. There's a lot of general-consumer excitement; maybe they've had an idea for a long time, and we have a lot of people who come to Bolt for that. But the way I view it is, we want to build tools that help professional builders of products, PMs, designers, engineers, to raise the ceiling of what they can do, and remove complexity, so instead of having to use coding agents in the CLI or whatever, we help you go from A to Z as fast as possible. That focus is where it matters. When we go into our conversations on the sales side, obviously all the other players, including the frontier labs, there are bake-offs that happen. But this is where the importance, and just generally for startups the importance, of really going deep on a specific ICP and workflows really matters. That's where we went, because we have a level of depth on certain workflows and capabilities, especially for product builders, that the other guys don't, because they're going very broad. So to use your analogy of OpenAI and Anthropic, we're taking a very Anthropic-type approach: really trying to make certain types of users and workflows within B2B usage insanely great, and we're not just spraying hundreds of millions of dollars at everything on the consumer side. Everyone Competing With Everyone: The Dotcom Parallel
zh: 这是个非常好的问题。过去一年，我想大概是大约一年前，我们做了一个决定：更加面向在企业里专业构建产品的人。有很多人对 AI 很兴奋。消费端有大量泛用户的热情；也许他们有一个想法已经很久了，我们有很多人就是为了这个来到 Bolt 的。但我的看法是，我们想打造能帮助专业的产品构建者——PM、设计师、工程师——抬高他们能力上限的工具，并且消除复杂性，让你不用去 CLI 或别的什么里用编程智能体，而是帮你以最快的速度从 A 走到 Z。这个聚焦才是关键所在。当我们进入销售侧的对话时，显然所有其他玩家，包括前沿实验室，都会有比稿竞争。但这就是为什么对一家创业公司来说，真正深耕一个特定的 ICP 和工作流如此重要。我们就是走的这条路，因为我们在某些工作流和能力上——尤其是面向产品构建者的——有其他公司没有的深度，因为他们走得太宽泛。所以借用你 OpenAI 和 Anthropic 的类比，我们走的是一条非常 Anthropic 式的路线：真正把 B2B 使用场景中的某些用户类型和工作流做到极致好，而不是在消费端把数亿美元到处乱撒。人人都在和所有人竞争：互联网泡沫的镜像

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
en: That's an interesting dichotomy. On the one hand, you want to grow the addressable market or the category by expanding, but at the same time you want to be remembered for something very specific that you do very, very well. I noticed you recently launched a slides capability; now you can also create interactive slides. You're also launching templates to make it easier for people to build apps, but that also creates new pockets of competition, right? The Canvas of the world, the Gammas of the world, suddenly become frenemies in a way, because you probably need to work with them too. So how are you thinking about that?
zh: 这是一个很有意思的二分法。一方面你想通过扩张来做大可触达市场或品类，但另一方面你又想被记住为某个非常具体、做得非常非常好的东西。我注意到你们最近上线了一个幻灯片功能；现在你还可以创建交互式幻灯片。你们也在上线模板，让人们更容易构建应用，但这也创造了新的竞争缝隙，对吧？Canvas 这些公司、Gamma 这些公司，突然间在某种程度上成了亦敌亦友的存在，因为你可能也需要和他们合作。所以你是怎么考虑这件事的？

speaker: Eric Simons
en: Yeah, I was on a podcast with one of the Gamma founders a week or two ago. It was the week we launched slides, and he said, "Oh yeah, I saw you guys launched slides," live on the podcast, and I kind of forgot that we had launched it, because for us it was just a fun project we made for ourselves. It's not like we're trying to get into the business of slides. But we ended up talking on the podcast about how everyone's competing with everyone. What I said to him, which I'll repeat here, is I don't think it's bad. We added some unique ideas into the mix as far as slides go. The reason we even launched it is that as a product, if you're an innovative company, you're going to have ideas, and you want to put them out there. If you've got the skills to do it, it's fun. And we open-sourced it too; it's not a closed-source thing. But I look back at the dotcom era, and there was a lot of this thinking where everyone was competing with everyone on everything, and everyone was trying to do everything. Back then it was portals, like Yahoo and AOL. "Media is coming to the internet, we have to have media. People need a home page of the internet, we need to be Yahoo or AOL, and we're going to do all these things. Oh yeah, search is just this tiny box up there, but it's the portal." Except, no, that tiny box was the juggernaut. That was the focal point. Google was like, "All this other stuff, forget it, just the input box: how do we make that thing insanely good and the best in the world?" And that was actually right underneath the other guys' noses, but they were so unfocused that they completely missed it. That, to me, is the era we're in. I look back historically, and maybe this time is different, but the comps don't track. We're in the middle of this, so it may seem like this time is different, until it's clear that this time isn't different, and certain companies break away because they actually focused. That's how we view our product strategy. It's not to say we won't release things that would be competitive with Gamma or whatever, but even on this product, both sides are cool: it's open source, you use it with any agent. On the flip side, I don't know Gamma's full feature suite. They've certainly got a ton of stuff we don't, and probably never will, and that's cool. That's why you'd want to use those guys. That's their entire product, so surely there's depth there.
zh: 是的，一两周前我和 Gamma 的一位创始人一起上了一个播客。那是我们上线幻灯片功能的那一周，他在播客直播中说，「哦对，我看到你们上线了幻灯片功能」，而我居然忘了我们上线过这个，因为对我们来说它只是一个我们给自己做的好玩项目。我们并不是想进军幻灯片业务。但我们在播客里聊到了「人人都在和所有人竞争」这个话题。我当时跟他说的话，我在这里再重复一遍：我不认为这是坏事。就幻灯片而言，我们加入了一些独特的想法。我们之所以上线它，是因为作为一款产品，如果你是一家有创新力的公司，你就会有想法，你会想把它发布出去。如果你有这个能力，那挺好玩的。而且我们把它开源了；这不是闭源的东西。但回看互联网泡沫时代，有很多这样的思维方式：所有人在所有事上和所有人竞争，每个人都想什么都做。当时是门户网站，像 Yahoo 和 AOL。「媒体正在上互联网，我们必须有媒体。人们需要一个互联网首页，我们要成为 Yahoo 或 AOL,我们要做所有这些事情。哦对了，搜索只是上面那个小框而已，但门户才是重点。」结果呢，不，那个小框才是真正的巨无霸。那才是焦点。Google 说，「其他的东西都忘掉吧，就那个输入框：我们怎么把那个东西做到极致好、做到世界最好？」而这件事其实就发生在其他那些公司的眼皮底下，但他们太不聚焦了，完全错过了。对我来说，这就是我们当下所处的时代。我回看历史，也许这次不一样，但这些先例对不上。我们身在其中，所以可能觉得这次不一样，直到人们看清这次并没有什么不同，某些公司因为真正聚焦而脱颖而出。这就是我们看待产品策略的方式。这不代表我们不会发布和 Gamma 或别的谁竞争的东西，但即便看这个产品，两方面都很酷：它开源，你可以搭配任何智能体使用。反过来，我也不了解 Gamma 完整的功能套件。他们肯定有很多我们没有、可能永远也不会有的东西，这很酷。这就是为什么你会想用他们。那是他们的全部产品，所以那里面肯定有深度。

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
en: The positioning is also very clear in each of the products. You're starting from a vibe-coding solution for PMs and engineers; the other ones started as a solution for marketers. Eventually there are some points of convergence, but that doesn't mean you don't have your own identity. I've seen this movie play out even in the product-tech category, which didn't even exist before. There was Optimizely doing A/B testing for marketers, and designers using Photoshop, and suddenly you start seeing tools created specifically for PMs. Back in the day, the whole winning strategy was that you have to be hyper, hyper specific: analytics, prototyping, road-mapping. And now it's about a platform instead of a portal. Now the game is the all-in-one platform, and everybody's overlapping. At the same time, they're also integrating, because they're assuming a lot of these enterprises are using different point solutions, and the winner, in a way, needs to let the data flow.
zh: 定位在每一款产品中也都非常清晰。你是从一个面向 PM 和工程师的 vibe coding 解决方案起步的；其他的则是从面向营销人员的解决方案起步的。最终会有一些交汇点，但这不代表你没有自己的身份。我甚至见过这部电影在产品技术品类里上演过——这个品类以前根本不存在。有 Optimizely 给营销人员做 A/B 测试，设计师用 Photoshop,突然间你开始看到专为 PM 打造的工具。在过去，整个制胜策略是你必须超级、超级细分：分析、原型、路线图。而现在则是平台而不是门户。现在这场游戏是一体化平台，所有人都在重叠。与此同时，他们也在做集成，因为他们假设很多企业正在使用各种不同的单点解决方案，而赢家在某种程度上需要让数据流动起来。

speaker: Eric Simons
en: It reminds me of the quote from the old Netscape CEO. His name slips my mind, but he said there are only two ways to make money in the software business: bundling and unbundling. These things go in phases: bundling will happen, and then unbundling. Streaming services are an excellent example. Netflix really rose to prominence by bundling, and people were like, "Okay, I don't have to buy all these subscriptions." And now there's a whole bunch of streaming services, so everything is getting unbundled. Typically it becomes clear that unbundling is where the value is going to be once there's too much bundling going on. That's kind of the issue, and I think we're approaching that in the market, if not already there in certain parts. The Case for Open Weights
zh: 这让我想起老 Netscape CEO 的那句话。他的名字我一时想不起来，但他说过，在软件行业，赚钱的方式只有两种：打包和解包。这些事情是分阶段轮回的：打包会发生，然后是解包。流媒体服务就是一个极好的例子。Netflix 真正是靠打包崛起的，人们说，「好，我不用买这么多订阅了。」而现在有一大堆流媒体服务，于是所有东西又开始解包。通常，当打包过度的时候，人们才会看清价值会流向解包那边。这就是问题所在，而我觉得我们正在市场上接近这个临界点，某些领域甚至已经到了。开放权重的主张

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
en: Another thing you mentioned briefly is open source, and I think that's a big deal here. You recently signed the open weights letter created by Microsoft, and you connect with so many different models. So I want to hear more about your take.
zh: 你刚才还简短提到了开源，我觉得在这里这是件大事。你最近签署了由 Microsoft 发起的开放权重公开信，而且你们接入了这么多不同的模型。所以我想多听听你的看法。

speaker: Eric Simons
en: Yeah. StackBlitz as a company has been deeply, deeply invested in open-source software since we were founded, and that's not even just lip service. We've put substantial amounts of money, even when we were not profitable, behind open source. There's a project called Vite, which is pretty much how everyone does web development these days, and we were the earliest backer of that. We hired people onto our team to just work on that full time, in open source. So as far as our roots to this stuff, and if you look at the open weights models, it's key that these things remain available and usable to all companies and all people around the world. There are a number of reasons for this. I looked at past parallels: I think back to the 90s, with Windows versus Linux, and the amount of innovation that has come. By the way, Windows is fine, Windows is used everywhere and doing great, and they've added a lot of value to this world. But Linux has been a workhorse for the hyperscalers we have, our ability to spin up micro-VMs, everything. And back then, these same things were being said, like, "Hey, Linux maybe should be outlawed." Crazy stuff in retrospect. And it reminds me a lot of now. So if you fast forward ten or twenty years and look back at where the bulk of the world's innovation is and what it's being powered by, I'd be surprised if open weights models were not a key pillar of that story. Geopolitically, I think it's a very bad idea, if Western countries were to try to bifurcate the open-source models coming from non-Western states, restricting their availability within Western states and forcing use of frontier labs. It does not appear we're doing this at this point, but that tends not to be a good recipe for how, at a national level, countries actually play to win. You see a lot of great companies in the States doing incredible things with these open models. There are some companies I've talked to recently doing really great research on how to optimize open-source models to run at a fraction of the cost. Imagine running Kimi K2 at one-tenth the current price. It's possible, if not 90%, then 80% off the list price, because they have access to the weights. If you don't have access to open model weights people can use, no innovation happens. If those guys crack that nut, it's going to be transformative for the level of ubiquitous, affordable access to these models. So to me, it's unfathomable that we would cut off that kind of innovation, but that's what would happen if open weights models were not permitted to be used.
zh: 好的。StackBlitz 作为一家公司，从创立之初就深深地、深深地投入在开源软件上，而且这绝不只是嘴上说说。我们在开源上投入了大量资金，甚至在我们还不盈利的时候。有一个叫 Vite 的项目，如今几乎所有人的 Web 开发都靠它，而我们是最早的支持者。我们把人招进团队全职做那个开源项目。所以从我们的根源来看，再看看开放权重模型，关键在于这些东西必须对所有公司、全世界所有人保持可用。这有很多原因。我回看过往的类似情形：我回想 90 年代，Windows 对 Linux,以及后来涌现的巨量创新。顺便说一句，Windows 挺好的，Windows 到处都在用，做得很好，他们为这个世界创造了很多价值。但 Linux 一直是我们今天这些超大规模云厂商的功臣，是我们能拉起微型虚拟机的基础，是一切。而在当年，同样的话也有人说过，比如，「嘿，Linux 也许应该被立法禁止。」现在回头看真是疯狂。这和现在非常像。所以如果你快进十年、二十年，回头看世界上大部分创新在哪里、由什么驱动，如果开放权重模型不是这个故事的关键支柱之一，我会很惊讶。从地缘政治角度说，如果西方国家试图把来自非西方国家的开源模型做分叉切断，限制它们在西方国家内的可用性，强迫人们使用前沿实验室的模型，我认为那是一个非常糟糕的主意。目前来看我们似乎没有这样做，但从国家层面讲，这不是各国真正想赢的打法。你看到美国有很多出色的公司在用这些开放模型做不可思议的事情。我最近和一些公司聊过，他们在做非常出色的工作，研究如何优化开源模型、让它以极低的成本运行。想象一下以现价的十分之一运行 Kimi K2。这是可能的，就算不是便宜 90%,也能比标价便宜 80%,因为他们能拿到权重。如果人们拿不到可以使用的开放模型权重，创新就不会发生。如果那帮人攻克了那个难题，对这种触手可及、人人用得起的模型访问来说，将是变革性的。所以对我来说，切断这种创新是不可想象的，但如果开放权重模型不被允许使用，这就是会发生的事。

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
en: The way I think about this is that it's much riskier to not participate in the open-source game than to participate in it. I think about your product as an application layer on top of a ton of models, and I kind of trust you, in some cases, to make the right decision and pick the models that optimize for my use case as well as my price sensitivity.
zh: 我对这个问题的看法是，不参与开源这场游戏，比参与其中风险大得多。我把你的产品看作是构建在大量模型之上的应用层，而且在某些情况下我有点信任你，相信你会做出正确的决策，选出既优化我的用例、又匹配我价格敏感度的模型。

speaker: Eric Simons
en: Exactly. Price is a really important thing, where the open weights models allow us to give more value to our customers at a lower price. So you're hurting customers, you're hurting the people trying to use AI, if these models can't be used. And of course there's the ability for us to use our own data to better tune the open weights models so they better fit the workloads our customers are doing. Cursor has been the phenomenal example of this with their Composer models, and that moves the needle to a way better experience at a fraction of the price. Getting Aggressive on Pricing
zh: 完全正确。价格是非常重要的东西，开放权重模型让我们能以更低的价格给客户更多价值。所以如果这些模型不能被使用，你伤害的是客户，是那些想用 AI 的人。当然，还有一点是我们可以用自己的数据去更好地微调开放权重模型，让它们更贴合客户正在跑的工作负载。Cursor 用他们的 Composer 模型就是这方面的绝佳范例，那把体验提升到了一个高得多的水平，而价格只是零头。定价上要更激进

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
en: So how are you thinking about pricing for your own product?
zh: 那你们对自己产品的定价是怎么考虑的？

speaker: Eric Simons
en: Good question. For us, we want to get really aggressive on pricing. The big sea change happening here is that open-source models are really catching up with the labs. There's a very tiny, I wouldn't even call it last mile at this point, but a last bit of distance to really marry these things where we can provide the same level of experience. Some number of weeks from now, we're going to be rolling out some stuff that will be our first foray into this, where we can offer things at price points that just would not have been possible before, while providing a great experience. We're all in on giving our users the most bang for the buck. That's how we've approached this from the get-go: when we figure out ways to reduce costs, which is always a top concern for us, it's not just for us as a business, it's really more about how we can make this a better economical decision for the folks using the product. We're always trying to figure out how to make it better and more affordable. Apologizing for the SaaS Apocalypse
zh: 好问题。对我们来说，我们想在定价上变得非常激进。这里正在发生的巨大变化是，开源模型真的在追赶那些实验室。现在距离我们能够提供同样水平的体验，只剩非常小的一步——我甚至不会称之为「最后一公里」了，而是最后一小段距离。从现在起的几周内，我们会推出一些东西，这将是我们在这方面的第一次尝试，我们能以以前根本不可能的价格点提供产品，同时保证出色的体验。我们全力投入在给用户最高的性价比上。我们从一开始就是这样做的：当我们找到降成本的方法时——成本始终是我们的头等大事——这不仅关乎我们作为一家企业，更多是在想我们如何让使用这款产品的人获得一个更划算的经济决策。我们一直在想办法让它更好、更便宜。为 SaaS 末日道歉

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
en: Speaking of pricing and being aggressive: the other day I was driving around and I saw a billboard by your company that said "Sorry, SaaS." So I want to hear your take on this apocalypse, and how these previous pricing models are probably not going to cut it, and what you're thinking about to make sure you end up on the winning side.
zh: 说到定价和激进：前几天我开车在路上，看到你们公司的一块广告牌，上面写着「Sorry, SaaS」。所以我想听听你对这场末日的看法，为什么以前的定价模式恐怕撑不住了，以及你在做些什么来确保自己站在赢的那一边。

speaker: Eric Simons
en: Yeah, for sure. So we're doing this whole campaign. We have all these billboards in New York and San Francisco that say "Sorry, SaaS." We're apologizing for the SaaS apocalypse. I think the per-seat model is the biggest risk point for SaaS businesses. With agents, as agents become more capable and powerful, you may not need as many seats for certain types of products. Not because those people won't be at the company, but because you're going to have agents going and doing things, and it makes a lot more sense to charge based on usage and access. When we launched Bolt, I'm very proud of our team, we got a lot of things right that ended up being how the industry now works. At that time, all these AI tools were, for whatever reason, charging like Netflix does: one price, all you can eat. Except in the case of these AI things, if you eat too much, we're going to throttle you and make you come back later, but it's 20 bucks a month. Copilot was doing that, Cursor was doing that, everyone was doing this. When we launched Bolt, the demand was so nuts that in the first 24 or 48 hours, people ripped through our subscription, which was like nine bucks at the time, in not even a day, and they were like, "I want to give you more money." So within 72 hours, we shipped usage-based pricing, where you could upgrade to the amount of usage you wanted. Within a few weeks of that, Barclays, an investment banking outfit, wrote a report they sent to their whole client base that said, "We think this model, that this random company StackBlitz, Bolt, has, is actually going to end up being how this stuff gets priced." And that is exactly what has happened. All these AI products, everyone's charging based on usage. In the case of Claude, they have the $20 plan, the $100 plan, the $200 plan. That's what we pioneered. I think that's just going to continue, where it's, "How do you charge based on the value being provided?" versus, "Oh hey, you have 10,000 people at your company, and if you want them to log in and use this, they're going to have to pay." It's, how much value are all those people getting out of this? Because if the value isn't there, what's probably going to happen is people are going to use their agents to hit your APIs, and then there are going to be three people at your company who actually need to use your product, and 2,000 who are getting it through an agent via the API. So you have to go, "Okay, how do we actually price the value?" To me it's actually kind of healthy. To be in the incumbent position is of course uncomfortable, but such is the nature of free markets. The reason those margins are under pressure is not because this stuff is bad. What we're seeing is that people are not losing their jobs because of AI, at least not to the degree some AI leaders said it was going to happen. What's actually going on is it's bringing into question the value of all these seats you're forcing people to buy. In a lot of cases it was really more of, "Well, we have to do it," not because we're getting that much value. So that comes back to you, and then you need to go innovate. That's my view on this side of things. Sharing Risk and Reward on Value
zh: 是的，当然。我们在做这整个营销活动。我们在纽约和旧金山有这么多块广告牌，上面写着「Sorry, SaaS」。我们在为 SaaS 末日道歉。我认为按席位收费模式是 SaaS 生意最大的风险点。随着智能体变得越来越能干、越来越强大，某些类型的产品你可能不再需要那么多席位。不是因为那些人不在公司了，而是因为会有智能体去替人做事，按使用量和访问量收费合理得多。当我们上线 Bolt 的时候，我为我们团队感到非常骄傲，我们做对了很多事情，后来整个行业都是这么运作的。当时，所有这些 AI 工具，不知道为什么，都在像 Netflix 那样收费：一个价格，随便用。只不过换成这些 AI 产品的情形，如果你用得太多，我们会限流让你稍后再来，但月费就是 20 美元。Copilot 是这么干的，Cursor 是这么干的，所有人都这么干。我们上线 Bolt 的时候，需求疯狂到在最初的 24 或 48 小时里，人们把我们的订阅套餐——当时大概九美元——用穿了连一天都不到，然后他们说，「我想给你更多钱。」所以在 72 小时内，我们上线了基于用量的定价，你可以升级到想要的使用量。在那之后几周内，巴克莱，一家投行，写了一份报告发给他们的全部客户，说，「我们认为这家叫 StackBlitz 的、籍籍无名的公司，Bolt,所采用的这种模式，最终会成为这类产品的定价方式。」而这正是后来发生的。所有这些 AI 产品，所有人都在按用量收费。以 Claude 为例，他们有 20 美元档、100 美元档、200 美元档。这是我们开创的。我认为这会继续下去，核心是「你如何按所提供的价值收费？」而不是「哦嘿，你们公司有一万人，如果你想让他们登录使用，他们每个人都得付费。」而是，这所有人从这个东西里获得了多少价值？因为如果没有那个价值，大概率会发生的是，人们会用他们的智能体去打你的 API,然后你公司里真正需要用你产品的只剩三个人，而有两千人通过智能体经 API 获取。所以你必须去想，「好，我们到底该怎么按价值定价？」对我来说这其实是挺健康的。身处被挑战的在位者位置当然不舒服，但自由市场的本质就是如此。那些利润率承压，不是因为这些东西不好。我们看到的是，人们并没有因为 AI 而失去工作，至少没有达到某些 AI 领袖所说的那种程度。实际正在发生的是，它让所有这些你强迫人们购买的席位的价值受到质疑。在很多情况下，那更多是「好吧，我们不得不买」，而不是因为我们真的获得了那么多价值。所以问题回到了你身上，然后你需要去创新。这就是我对这一面的看法。在价值上共担风险与回报

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
en: We're seeing this across the board. Back in the day, B2B SaaS was mostly a captive audience, because first of all, the person buying the thing is not using the thing, which is already a yellow flag. But also, usage was only being measured maybe the week before renewals, where all these customer success managers had to prove, "Hey, someone in the company did something very good, hence we did 12 more months of grace." And now you're on the hook, and you're sharing risk and reward, but ultimately the access to value and usage is right there for everybody.
zh: 我们在各行各业都看到了这一点。在过去，B2B SaaS 基本上是一群被捆绑的用户，因为首先，掏钱买的人不是用它的人，这本身就已经是一个黄色警报了。而且使用量只在续约前一周左右才被测量，所有这些客户成功经理都得证明，「嘿，公司里有人用得很好，所以我们再续 12 个月吧。」而现在你要自己负起责任，你在共担风险与回报，但归根结底，通往价值和用量的入口就摆在那儿，人人可见。

speaker: Eric Simons
en: Exactly. To me it's just a good fattening of margins where value was not tremendously present. Because then you see other SaaS companies that are crushing it, like Shopify. Early on there's an over-rotation, "all of SaaS is done," and so on. But what's really going on? There was a pending question of, okay, which of these things, is it clear any of them are going to be able to thread the needle here? And now we're seeing the first crops of these where it's like, yeah, these guys are doing great. Those are the gold standards other SaaS companies have to look up to and go, "Okay, this is how we have to approach the problem." It's a similar sea change to what happened during the dotcom era, where the traditional media and print companies faced these same questions. Some threaded the needle really well, some did not. But such is life and business: how good are you at embracing pain quickly, and then pushing through it and figuring out what needs to be done?
zh: 完全正确。对我来说，这只是在那些价值并不怎么真实存在的地方，一次健康的利润率挤水分。因为同时你也看到其他 SaaS 公司干得风生水起，比如 Shopify。早期会有过度反应，「SaaS 全完蛋了」之类的。但真实的情况是什么？本来有一个悬而未决的问题：这些东西里面，到底有没有哪家能明确地穿针引线渡过这一关？而现在我们看到了第一批成果，就是那种， yeah,这些家伙干得非常好。那些就是其他 SaaS 公司必须仰望并自问的黄金标准，「好，这就是我们必须应对这个问题的方式。」这和互联网泡沫时代发生的变化类似，当时的传统媒体和印刷出版公司面对过同样的问题。有的把针穿得非常好，有的没有。但生活和生意就是这样：你有多擅长快速拥抱痛苦，然后挺过去、想清楚该做什么？

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
en: That's a beautiful way to wrap up this conversation. Thank you so much for your time, Eric. It's been a pleasure to learn from you.
zh: 这真是一个为这场对话收尾的绝妙方式。非常感谢你抽出时间，Eric。向你学习非常愉快。

speaker: Eric Simons
en: Yeah, thank you for having me. It's been a blast.
zh: 是的，谢谢你们邀请我。聊得非常尽兴。
